sentences.text: This dinosaur stood about two meters tall when walking on four legs, with its belly only seventy centimeters above the ground.
Its snout was wide at the tip, measuring roughly twenty centimeters, and expanded to thirty centimeters at the base.
Although no actual teeth survived in the fossil record, the skull contained sockets for ten rows of teeth within a span of nineteen point five centimeters.
Based on the proportions of the skull bones, the entire head likely measured eighty-three point three centimeters in length.
The hand possessed a large spike on the thumb, while the forelimbs were only sixty percent the size of the hind legs.
The lower leg bone was very short compared to the thigh bone, measuring seventy-seven point seven centimeters against ninety-one centimeters.
Its neck was quite long, reaching about one point six meters because it had more and longer neck vertebrae than related species.
The foot structure was unique because the long foot bones did not touch each other, suggesting a thick pad of flesh supported most of the weight.
It may be the first known ornithischian dinosaur to possess graviportal anatomy, a body plan built for moving slowly while carrying a massive weight.
Because of its unusual shape, early researchers thought it might look somewhat like an ankylosaur.
The original specimen was found in 1965 by Philippe Taquet at the Gadoufaoua site in the Tenere desert of Niger.
Taquet and Dale Russell formally described the species in 1999 and named it Lurdusaurus arenatus.
Before the official name was assigned, the animal was informally called Gravisaurus tenerensis by Chabli in 1988.
The name combines a word meaning heavy with another meaning sandy, referencing the desert where the fossils were found.
The large claws on its thumbs could have been deadly weapons, capable of causing fatal injuries to a predator if they struck the neck or side.
Its low and deep body prevented it from running fast, but the low center of gravity allowed it to spin quickly in tight circles to face a threat.
Tom Holtz has suggested that this animal might have lived in or near water, similar to a hippopotamus.
The rock layers and nearby aquatic animals indicate it lived in a freshwater river environment with a humid tropical climate.
The genus was established by Taquet and Russell in 1999.
A synonym for the species is Gravisaurus tenerensis, proposed by Chabli in 1988.
It belongs to the larger group known as Iguanodontoidea.
Gregory S. Paul argued in 2008 that it is not closely related to Lanzhousaurus because of differences in the prepubic process, though this idea cannot be fully tested without more complete bones.
Taquet agreed in 2012 that the animal falls outside the family Iguanodontidae but remained uncertain about its exact relationship to other members of that group.
Recent work by Gônet, Allain, and Houssaye in 2026 interpreted the animal as an obligate quadruped, meaning it walked exclusively on four legs.
This creature lived in Africa during the middle Cretaceous period, between one hundred twenty-one and one hundred twelve million years ago.
The fossils date to the late Aptian and early Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous, approximately one hundred twelve million years ago.
The genus time range is recorded as the Albian stage, spanning from one hundred thirteen point two to one hundred point five million years ago.
